keyPoints: Vec a is $[4, 3]$ with magnitude $5$ and unit vector $[0.8, 0.6]$
Scalar multiples $k \vec{a}$ are parallel, sign of $k$ gives direction
Orthogonal vector is $[-3, 4]$
modelAnswer: Take $\vec{a} = 4 \hat{\imath} + 3 \hat{\jmath}$, so $\vec{a} = [4, 3]$ and $|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{16 + 9} = 5$. Any vector that is a scalar multiple of $\vec{a}$ is parallel to $\vec{a}$: $2 \vec{a} = [8, 6]$ is twice as long in the same direction, $-\vec{a} = [-4, -3]$ is opposite, $0.5 \vec{a} = [2, 1.5]$ is half length. The unit vector in the direction of $\vec{a}$ is $\vec{a}/|\vec{a}| = (4/5) \hat{\imath} + (3/5) \hat{\jmath} = [0.8, 0.6]$. A vector perpendicular to $\vec{a}$ can be obtained by swapping and negating one component, for example $[-3, 4]$ is orthogonal to $[4, 3]$. The other vectors in the figure are each of the form $k \vec{a}$ for some scalar $k$, and their lengths are $|k|$ times $5$ and their directions are the same as $\vec{a}$ when $k$ is positive and opposite when $k$ is negative. This covers all subparts that ask to express vectors in terms of $\vec{a}$.

keyPoints: $\overrightarrow{AB} = \vec{a}$ and $\overrightarrow{AD} = \vec{b}$ gives $\overrightarrow{DC} = \vec{a}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC} = \vec{b}$
$\overrightarrow{AC} = \vec{a} + \vec{b}$ and $\overrightarrow{BD} = -\vec{a} + \vec{b}$ by triangle law
$\overrightarrow{AO} = (\vec{a}+\vec{b})/2$ and $\overrightarrow{BO} = (-\vec{a}+\vec{b})/2$, $\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{AC} = 2\vec{a}+\vec{b}$
modelAnswer: Let $\overrightarrow{AB} = \vec{a}$ and $\overrightarrow{AD} = \vec{b}$, with $A$ at the origin. Then vertices are $A=0$, $B=\vec{a}$, $D=\vec{b}$, $C=\vec{a}+\vec{b}$. Opposite sides are equal and parallel, so $\overrightarrow{DC} = \overrightarrow{AB} = \vec{a}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC} = \overrightarrow{AD} = \vec{b}$, while $\overrightarrow{DA} = -\vec{b}$ and $\overrightarrow{CD} = -\vec{a}$ by direction. Diagonal $\overrightarrow{AC} = \overrightarrow{AB} + \overrightarrow{AD} = \vec{a} + \vec{b}$ by triangle law. Diagonal $\overrightarrow{DB} = \overrightarrow{AB} - \overrightarrow{AD} = \vec{a} - \vec{b}$, and $\overrightarrow{BD} = -\overrightarrow{DB} = -\vec{a} + \vec{b}$. Let $O$ be the intersection of the diagonals, so $\overrightarrow{AO} = (\vec{a}+\vec{b})/2$. Then $\overrightarrow{BO} = \overrightarrow{AO} - \overrightarrow{AB} = (-\vec{a} + \vec{b})/2$, and similarly $\overrightarrow{CO} = -(\vec{a}+\vec{b})/2$ and $\overrightarrow{DO} = (\vec{a} - \vec{b})/2$ but magnitudes are the same. Adding vectors: $\overrightarrow{AB} + \overrightarrow{AC} = \vec{a} + (\vec{a}+\vec{b}) = 2\vec{a} + \vec{b}$. These give all seven requested expressions in terms of $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$.

keyPoints: The midpoint's position vector is the average of the two endpoints' position vectors: OM = (OP+OQ)/2.
PQ = OQ - OP, and since M bisects PQ, PM = (1/2)PQ and QM = -PM.
modelAnswer:
$\overrightarrow{OP}=\vec p+\vec q$, $\overrightarrow{OQ}=\vec p-\vec q$, M is the midpoint of PQ so $\overrightarrow{OM}=\dfrac{\overrightarrow{OP}+\overrightarrow{OQ}}{2}$.

i. $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\overrightarrow{OQ}-\overrightarrow{OP}=(\vec p-\vec q)-(\vec p+\vec q)=-2\vec q$

ii. $\overrightarrow{PM}=\tfrac12\overrightarrow{PQ}=-\vec q$

iii. $\overrightarrow{QM}=-\overrightarrow{PM}=\vec q$ (since M is the midpoint, QM = -PM)

iv. $\overrightarrow{OM}=\dfrac{(\vec p+\vec q)+(\vec p-\vec q)}{2}=\vec p$

keyPoints: Resolving each vector into (east, north) components using bearing angle, then adding the components, gives the resultant velocity/speed and bearing for a wind-drift problem.
modelAnswer:
Bearing is measured clockwise from north, so a bearing $\theta$ speed $v$ gives components $[v\sin\theta, v\cos\theta]$ (east, north).

Plane: $380[\sin45^{\circ},\cos45^{\circ}]=380[0.7071,0.7071]\approx[268.7,268.7]$

Wind: $50[\sin135^{\circ},\cos135^{\circ}]=50[0.7071,-0.7071]\approx[35.4,-35.4]$

Resultant (actual velocity) $\approx[268.7+35.4,\;268.7-35.4]=[304.1,233.3]$

Speed $=\sqrt{304.1^{2}+233.3^{2}}=\sqrt{92478+54448}\approx\sqrt{146926}\approx383.3$ mph

Bearing $=\arctan\!\left(\dfrac{304.1}{233.3}\right)\approx52.5^{\circ}$

So the airplane's actual velocity is about **383.3 mph at a bearing of approximately $52.5^{\circ}$**.

Other diagonal $=\vec u-\vec v=[1,4]$, length $=\sqrt{1+16}=\sqrt{17}$

The diagonals of the parallelogram have lengths $\sqrt{13}$ and $\sqrt{17}$ units.

keyPoints: Successive displacement legs at given bearings are resolved into (east, north) components and added; the resultant's magnitude and arctan give the final distance and bearing.
modelAnswer:
First leg: 15 km at bearing $30^{\circ}$: components $=15[\sin30^{\circ},\cos30^{\circ}]=15[0.5,0.866]=[7.5,12.99]$

Second leg: 8 km due west: components $=[-8,0]$

Total displacement $=[7.5-8,\;12.99+0]=[-0.5,12.99]$

Distance from dry port $=\sqrt{0.25+168.7}=\sqrt{168.99}\approx13.0$ km

Bearing: since the x-component is slightly negative (west of north) and y is positive, bearing $=360^{\circ}-\arctan\!\left(\dfrac{0.5}{12.99}\right)\approx360^{\circ}-2.2^{\circ}=357.8^{\circ}$

So the truck is about **13.0 km from the dry port, at a bearing of approximately $357.8^{\circ}$** (nearly due north).

ii. $2\vec a-3\vec b=(6-6)\hat\imath+(10+12)\hat\jmath=22\hat\jmath$

iii. $5(2\vec a+\vec b)=5[(6+2)\hat\imath+(10-4)\hat\jmath]=5(8\hat\imath+6\hat\jmath)=40\hat\imath+30\hat\jmath$

iv. $0.5(\vec a-\vec b)=0.5[(3-2)\hat\imath+(5+4)\hat\jmath]=0.5\hat\imath+4.5\hat\jmath$

v. $|\vec a+\vec b|$: $\vec a+\vec b=[5,1]$, $|\cdot|=\sqrt{26}$

vi. $|\vec a-\vec b|$: $\vec a-\vec b=[1,9]$, $|\cdot|=\sqrt{82}$

vii. $|\vec a|+2|\vec b|$: $|\vec a|=\sqrt{9+25}=\sqrt{34}$, $|\vec b|=\sqrt{4+16}=2\sqrt5$. Sum $=\sqrt{34}+4\sqrt5$

viii. $|\vec a|-|\vec b|=\sqrt{34}-2\sqrt5$

keyPoints: Computing side vectors and their squared magnitudes lets you test the Pythagorean relation (right angle) or equal side lengths (isosceles) without any drawing.
modelAnswer:
i. $A(0,2), B(\sqrt3,-1), C(0,-2)$: $\overrightarrow{AB}=[\sqrt3,-3]$, $|\overrightarrow{AB}|^2=3+9=12$. $\overrightarrow{BC}=[-\sqrt3,-1]$, $|\overrightarrow{BC}|^2=3+1=4$. $\overrightarrow{CA}=[0,4]$, $|\overrightarrow{CA}|^2=16$. Since $12+4=16=|CA|^2$, the triangle satisfies the Pythagorean relation with the right angle at B, so **ABC is a right-angled triangle**.

ii. $A(3,1), B(-2,-3), C(2,2)$: $\overrightarrow{AB}=[-5,-4]$, $|\overrightarrow{AB}|^2=25+16=41$. $\overrightarrow{BC}=[4,5]$, $|\overrightarrow{BC}|^2=16+25=41$. Since $|AB|=|BC|=\sqrt{41}$, two sides are equal, so **ABC is an isosceles triangle**.

keyPoints: Matching i-hat and j-hat coefficients on both sides of a vector equation gives a pair of simultaneous linear equations in the unknown scalars, solved by substitution or elimination.
modelAnswer:
$\vec a=3\hat\imath-2\hat\jmath$, $\vec b=\hat\imath+4\hat\jmath$. $x\vec a+y\vec b=(3x+y)\hat\imath+(-2x+4y)\hat\jmath=4\hat\imath-12\hat\jmath$.

So $3x+y=4$ and $-2x+4y=-12$.

From the first equation, $y=4-3x$. Substituting: $-2x+4(4-3x)=-12\Rightarrow-2x+16-12x=-12\Rightarrow-14x=-28\Rightarrow x=2$.

Then $y=4-3(2)=-2$.

So $x=2, y=-2$.

keyPoints: A unit vector is obtained by dividing a vector by its own magnitude: u-hat = u / |u|.
modelAnswer:
i. $\overrightarrow{PQ}$, $P(1,4), Q(4,8)$: $\overrightarrow{PQ}=[3,4]$, $|\overrightarrow{PQ}|=\sqrt{9+16}=5$. Unit vector $=\left[\tfrac35,\tfrac45\right]$

ii. $\vec u=5\hat\imath-12\hat\jmath$: $|\vec u|=\sqrt{25+144}=13$. Unit vector $=\tfrac{5}{13}\hat\imath-\tfrac{12}{13}\hat\jmath$

iii. $\vec b=-6\hat\imath-8\hat\jmath$: $|\vec b|=\sqrt{36+64}=10$. Unit vector $=-\tfrac{6}{10}\hat\imath-\tfrac{8}{10}\hat\jmath=-\tfrac35\hat\imath-\tfrac45\hat\jmath$
stem:
Find the unit vectors of the following vectors.
(i) $\overrightarrow{P Q}$ when $\mathrm{P}(1,4), \mathrm{Q}(4,8)$
(ii) $\vec{u}=5 \hat{\imath}-12 \hat{\jmath}$
(iii) $\vec{b}=-6 \hat{\imath}-8 \hat{\jmath}$

keyPoints: Each part first combines the given vectors componentwise, then normalizes the result by dividing by its own magnitude.
modelAnswer:
$\vec a=2\hat\imath-4\hat\jmath$, $\vec b=\hat\imath-2\hat\jmath$, $\vec c=[1,3]$.

i. $\vec a+\vec b=[3,-6]$, $|\cdot|=\sqrt{9+36}=3\sqrt5$. Unit vector $=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}\hat\imath-\tfrac{2}{\sqrt5}\hat\jmath$

ii. $2\vec a-\vec c=[4,-8]-[1,3]=[3,-11]$, $|\cdot|=\sqrt{9+121}=\sqrt{130}$. Unit vector $=\tfrac{3}{\sqrt{130}}\hat\imath-\tfrac{11}{\sqrt{130}}\hat\jmath$

iii. $2\vec a-\vec b=[4,-8]-[1,-2]=[3,-6]$, $|\cdot|=3\sqrt5$. Unit vector $=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}\hat\imath-\tfrac{2}{\sqrt5}\hat\jmath$ (same direction as part i)

iv. $3(\vec a+\vec c)$: $\vec a+\vec c=[3,-1]$, times 3 $=[9,-3]$, $|\cdot|=\sqrt{81+9}=3\sqrt{10}$. Unit vector $=\tfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\hat\imath-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\hat\jmath$

v. $\vec a+\vec b+2\vec c=[3,-6]+[2,6]=[5,0]$, $|\cdot|=5$. Unit vector $=\hat\imath$

vi. $4\vec a-2\vec b+\vec c=[8,-16]-[2,-4]+[1,3]=[7,-9]$, $|\cdot|=\sqrt{49+81}=\sqrt{130}$. Unit vector $=\tfrac{7}{\sqrt{130}}\hat\imath-\tfrac{9}{\sqrt{130}}\hat\jmath$

(ii) $2 \vec{a}-\vec{c}$
(iii) $2 \vec{a}-\vec{b}$
(iv) $3(\vec{a}+\vec{c})$

modelAnswer:

i. $2\vec a-\vec b=[2,-6]-[2,4]=[0,-10]$, magnitude 10, unit vector $[0,-1]$. Vector of magnitude 4 in this direction $=4[0,-1]=[0,-4]=-4\hat\jmath$

ii. $\vec a+2\vec b=[1,-3]+[4,8]=[5,5]$, magnitude $5\sqrt2$, unit vector $\left[\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2},\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right]$. topicTitle: 7.2 Ratio Formula for Finding Position Vector of a Point on a Vector
keyPoints: For a parallelogram with adjacent side vectors u and v, its two diagonals are u+v and u-v; their lengths are the magnitudes of those sums/differences.
modelAnswer:
Adjacent sides of the parallelogram: $\vec u=2\hat\imath+\hat\jmath$ and $\vec v=\hat\imath-3\hat\jmath$.

One diagonal $=\vec u+\vec v=[3,-2]$, length $=\sqrt{9+4}=\sqrt{13}$

Other diagonal $=\vec u-\vec v=[1,4]$, length $=\sqrt{1+16}=\sqrt{17}$

The diagonals of the parallelogram have lengths $\sqrt{13}$ and $\sqrt{17}$ units.
stem: Use vectors to find the length of diagonals of a parallelogram having adjacent sides $2 \hat{\imath}+\hat{\jmath}$ and $\hat{\imath}-3 \hat{\jmath}$.

topicTitle: 7.2 Ratio Formula for Finding Position Vector of a Point on a Vector
keyPoints: Computing side vectors and their squared magnitudes lets you test the Pythagorean relation (right angle) or equal side lengths (isosceles) without any drawing.
modelAnswer:
i. $A(0,2), B(\sqrt3,-1), C(0,-2)$: $\overrightarrow{AB}=[\sqrt3,-3]$, $|\overrightarrow{AB}|^2=3+9=12$. $\overrightarrow{BC}=[-\sqrt3,-1]$, $|\overrightarrow{BC}|^2=3+1=4$. $\overrightarrow{CA}=[0,4]$, $|\overrightarrow{CA}|^2=16$. Since $12+4=16=|CA|^2$, the triangle satisfies the Pythagorean relation with the right angle at B, so **ABC is a right-angled triangle**.

ii. $A(3,1), B(-2,-3), C(2,2)$: $\overrightarrow{AB}=[-5,-4]$, $|\overrightarrow{AB}|^2=25+16=41$. $\overrightarrow{BC}=[4,5]$, $|\overrightarrow{BC}|^2=16+25=41$. Since $|AB|=|BC|=\sqrt{41}$, two sides are equal, so **ABC is an isosceles triangle**.
stem:
(i) Show that $A(0,2), B(\sqrt{3},-1), C(0,-2)$ are the vertices of a right-angled triangle.
(ii) Show that $A(3,1), B(-2,-3), C(2,2)$ are the vertices of an isosceles triangle.

topicTitle: 7.2 Ratio Formula for Finding Position Vector of a Point on a Vector
keyPoints: Three points are collinear exactly when the vector between any two pairs of them are parallel (scalar multiples of each other).
modelAnswer:
$P(-1,x), Q(3,2), R(7,3)$ collinear means $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ and $\overrightarrow{QR}$ are parallel.

$\overrightarrow{PQ}=[4,\,2-x]$, $\overrightarrow{QR}=[4,1]$.

Since the x-components already match (both 4), the scalar ratio is $\lambda=1$, so the y-components must also match: $2-x=1\Rightarrow x=1$.
stem: Find $x$, such that the points $P(-1, x), Q(3,2)$ and $R(7,3)$ are collinear.

topicTitle: 7.2 Ratio Formula for Finding Position Vector of a Point on a Vector
keyPoints: If two vectors AB and CD are equal, B can be recovered as A plus the known vector CD.
modelAnswer:
$\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{CD}$, $A(0,2), C(-2,4), D(-1,5)$.

$\overrightarrow{CD}=D-C=(-1-(-2),\,5-4)=[1,1]$

Since $\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{CD}$: $B=A+\overrightarrow{CD}=(0+1,\,2+1)=(1,3)$

topicTitle: 7.2 Ratio Formula for Finding Position Vector of a Point on a Vector
keyPoints: If both pairs of opposite sides of a quadrilateral are equal (as vectors, i.e. equal in magnitude AND direction), the quadrilateral is a parallelogram.
modelAnswer:
$\overrightarrow{EF}=\overrightarrow{HG}$ means side EF is equal in length and parallel to side HG (opposite sides of the quadrilateral EFGH). $\overrightarrow{EH}=\overrightarrow{FG}$ means side EH is equal in length and parallel to side FG (the other pair of opposite sides).

Since both pairs of opposite sides of EFGH are equal and parallel, **EFGH is a parallelogram**.
stem: What type of a quadrilateral $E F G H$ is if $\overrightarrow{E F}=\overrightarrow{H G}$ and $\overrightarrow{E H}=\overrightarrow{F G}$ ?

topicTitle: 7.2 Ratio Formula for Finding Position Vector of a Point on a Vector
keyPoints: The quadrilateral formed by joining consecutive midpoints of any quadrilateral's sides is always a parallelogram (Varignon's theorem), provable by showing one pair of its sides are equal as vectors.
modelAnswer:
$U(9,4), V(-7,7), W(-4,-7), X(5,-5)$.

Midpoints of the sides: $P=\text{mid}(UV)=(1,5.5)$, $Q=\text{mid}(VW)=(-5.5,0)$, $R=\text{mid}(WX)=(0.5,-6)$, $S=\text{mid}(XU)=(7,-0.5)$.

$\overrightarrow{PQ}=Q-P=(-6.5,-5.5)$ and $\overrightarrow{SR}=R-S=(-6.5,-5.5)$, so $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\overrightarrow{SR}$: one pair of opposite sides of PQRS is equal and parallel, which is sufficient to prove **PQRS is a parallelogram** (this is Varignon's midpoint theorem).
stem: Vertices of a quadrilateral are $U(9,4), V(-7,7), W(-4,-7)$ and $X(5,-5)$. Find mid points of its sides and prove that the figure obtained by joining mid points consecutively is a parallelogram.

topicTitle: 7.2 Ratio Formula for Finding Position Vector of a Point on a Vector
keyPoints: The midpoint's position vector is the average of the two endpoints' position vectors: OM = (OP+OQ)/2.
PQ = OQ - OP, and since M bisects PQ, PM = (1/2)PQ and QM = -PM.
modelAnswer:
$\overrightarrow{OP}=\vec p+\vec q$, $\overrightarrow{OQ}=\vec p-\vec q$, M is the midpoint of PQ so $\overrightarrow{OM}=\dfrac{\overrightarrow{OP}+\overrightarrow{OQ}}{2}$.

i. $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\overrightarrow{OQ}-\overrightarrow{OP}=(\vec p-\vec q)-(\vec p+\vec q)=-2\vec q$

ii. $\overrightarrow{PM}=\tfrac12\overrightarrow{PQ}=-\vec q$

iii. $\overrightarrow{QM}=-\overrightarrow{PM}=\vec q$ (since M is the midpoint, QM = -PM)

iv. $\overrightarrow{OM}=\dfrac{(\vec p+\vec q)+(\vec p-\vec q)}{2}=\vec p$
sectionLabel: Ratio Formula for Finding Position Vector of a Point on a Vector
stem:
Given that $\overrightarrow{O P}=\vec{p}+\vec{q}, \overrightarrow{O Q}=\vec{p}-\vec{q}$ and $M$ is mid-point of $\overrightarrow{P Q}$. Find in terms of $\vec{p}$ and $\vec{q}$.
(i) $\overrightarrow{P Q}$
(ii) $\overrightarrow{P M}$
(iii) $\overrightarrow{Q M}$
(iv) $\overrightarrow{O M}$

topicTitle: 7.2 Ratio Formula for Finding Position Vector of a Point on a Vector
keyPoints: The midpoint of a segment with endpoints having position vectors a and b is (a+b)/2.
DE = (1/2) BC follows directly from substituting the midpoint formulas for D and E, proving both the length-half and parallel properties at once.
modelAnswer:
Let triangle ABC have position vectors $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$, and let D, E be the midpoints of AB and AC respectively.

$D=\dfrac{\vec a+\vec b}{2}$, $E=\dfrac{\vec a+\vec c}{2}$ (midpoint position-vector formula).

$\overrightarrow{DE}=E-D=\dfrac{\vec a+\vec c}{2}-\dfrac{\vec a+\vec b}{2}=\dfrac{\vec c-\vec b}{2}=\tfrac12\overrightarrow{BC}$

So $\overrightarrow{DE}=\tfrac12\overrightarrow{BC}$, hence $|DE|=\tfrac12|BC|$ (and DE is parallel to BC). This proves the segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is half the length of the third side.
sectionLabel: Ratio Formula for Finding Position Vector of a Point on a Vector
stem: Prove that the line segments joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle are half in length of third side.

topicTitle: 7.2 Ratio Formula for Finding Position Vector of a Point on a Vector
keyPoints: Two vectors are parallel exactly when one is a scalar multiple of the other; showing MN = k*AB for some scalar k proves the parallelism directly.
modelAnswer:
Let trapezium ABCD have $\overrightarrow{AB}\parallel\overrightarrow{DC}$, with position vectors $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c,\vec d$, and M, N the midpoints of the two non-parallel sides AD and BC.

$M=\dfrac{\vec a+\vec d}{2}$, $N=\dfrac{\vec b+\vec c}{2}$.

Since $AB\parallel DC$, $\vec c-\vec d=\lambda(\vec b-\vec a)$ for some scalar $\lambda$.

$\overrightarrow{MN}=N-M=\dfrac{(\vec b-\vec a)+(\vec c-\vec d)}{2}=\dfrac{(\vec b-\vec a)+\lambda(\vec b-\vec a)}{2}=\dfrac{1+\lambda}{2}(\vec b-\vec a)$

So $\overrightarrow{MN}$ is a scalar multiple of $\overrightarrow{AB}$, hence **MN is parallel to both AB and DC**, the two parallel sides of the trapezium.
sectionLabel: Ratio Formula for Finding Position Vector of a Point on a Vector
stem: Prove that the joining the midpoints of the two non-parallel sides of a trapezium is parallel to its parallel sides.

topicTitle: 7.2 Ratio Formula for Finding Position Vector of a Point on a Vector
keyPoints: The intersection of the segment joining midpoints of two adjacent sides of a parallelogram with the corresponding diagonal always divides that diagonal in the ratio 1:3, provable via position vectors or verified by a concrete coordinate example.
modelAnswer:
Let a parallelogram ABCD have position vectors $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c,\vec d$ (so $\vec d=\vec a+\vec c-\vec b$, since diagonals bisect each other). Let M, N be the midpoints of adjacent sides AB and BC: $M=\dfrac{\vec a+\vec b}{2}$, $N=\dfrac{\vec b+\vec c}{2}$.

Parametrize line MN as $M+t(N-M)$ and diagonal BD as $\vec b+s(\vec d-\vec b)$, then match the (affinely independent) coefficients of $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ on both sides. Solving gives $t=\tfrac12$ and $s=\tfrac14$.

So the intersection point divides diagonal BD in the ratio $s:(1-s)=\tfrac14:\tfrac34=1:3$ from B.

Check with a concrete square $A(0,0),B(2,0),C(2,2),D(0,2)$: midpoint of AB is $(1,0)$, midpoint of BC is $(2,1)$; the line through them meets diagonal BD (from $(2,0)$ to $(0,2)$) at $(1.5,0.5)$, which is exactly $1/4$ of the way from B to D, confirming the $1:3$ ratio. Since a square and rectangle are both parallelograms, the same proof covers all three.
sectionLabel: Ratio Formula for Finding Position Vector of a Point on a Vector
stem: Prove that the line segment joining mid points of adjacent sides of a square or rectangle or parallelogram divides the corresponding diagonal in the ratio $1: 3$.

topicTitle: 7.2 Ratio Formula for Finding Position Vector of a Point on a Vector
keyPoints: The internal-division ratio formula r = (m*b + n*a)/(m+n) gives the position vector of the dividing point directly from the two endpoints' position vectors.
modelAnswer:
Position vectors $\vec c=3\hat\imath+2\hat\jmath$, $\vec d=\hat\imath-4\hat\jmath$. O divides CD in ratio $2:3$ internally, so using the ratio formula $\vec r=\dfrac{m\vec d+n\vec c}{m+n}$ with $m:n=2:3$:

$\vec r=\dfrac{2(\hat\imath-4\hat\jmath)+3(3\hat\imath+2\hat\jmath)}{5}=\dfrac{2\hat\imath-8\hat\jmath+9\hat\imath+6\hat\jmath}{5}=\dfrac{11\hat\imath-2\hat\jmath}{5}=\dfrac{11}{5}\hat\imath-\dfrac25\hat\jmath$
sectionLabel: Ratio Formula for Finding Position Vector of a Point on a Vector
stem: The position vectors of points C and D are $3 \hat{\imath}+2 \hat{\jmath}$ and $\hat{\imath}-4 \hat{\jmath}$ respectively. Find the position vector of point O dividing the line segment joining C and D in the ratio $2: 3$ internally.

topicTitle: 7.2 Ratio Formula for Finding Position Vector of a Point on a Vector
keyPoints: The two points that trisect a segment AB are A + (1/3)(B-A) and A + (2/3)(B-A), a direct extension of the ratio/section formula.
modelAnswer:
$\overrightarrow{OA}=-\hat\imath+3\hat\jmath$, i.e. $A(-1,3)$; $\overrightarrow{OB}=6\hat\imath+2\hat\jmath$, i.e. $B(6,2)$.

The two points trisecting AB are at $A+\tfrac13(B-A)$ and $A+\tfrac23(B-A)$, where $B-A=[7,-1]$.

$T_1=(-1+\tfrac73,\,3-\tfrac13)=\left(\tfrac43,\tfrac83\right)$

$T_2=(-1+\tfrac{14}3,\,3-\tfrac23)=\left(\tfrac{11}3,\tfrac73\right)$

So the points trisecting AB are $\left(\tfrac43,\tfrac83\right)$ and $\left(\tfrac{11}3,\tfrac73\right)$.
sectionLabel: Ratio Formula for Finding Position Vector of a Point on a Vector
stem: If $\overrightarrow{O A}=-\hat{\imath}+3 \hat{\jmath}, \overrightarrow{O B}=6 \hat{\imath}+2 \hat{\jmath}$, find the point trisecting the join of $\overrightarrow{A B}$.

topicTitle: 7.2 Ratio Formula for Finding Position Vector of a Point on a Vector
keyPoints: In any parallelogram, the diagonals bisect each other, so the midpoints of both diagonals must coincide -- this fixes the fourth vertex given the other three.
modelAnswer:
Parallelogram $ABCD$: $A(-3,0), B(1,-2), C(5,0)$. The diagonals AC and BD bisect each other, so $\text{midpoint}(AC)=\text{midpoint}(BD)$.

Midpoint of AC $=\left(\dfrac{-3+5}{2},\dfrac{0+0}{2}\right)=(1,0)$

Setting this equal to the midpoint of BD: $\left(\dfrac{1+D_x}{2},\dfrac{-2+D_y}{2}\right)=(1,0)\Rightarrow D_x=1, D_y=2$

So $D=(1,2)$.
sectionLabel: Ratio Formula for Finding Position Vector of a Point on a Vector
stem: Find the coordinates of vertex $D$ of a parallelogram $A B C D$ if $A(-3,0), B(1,-2)$ and $C(5,0)$ are its three vertices.
